Hedley Ashcombe.narrative: I've worked the terrace strips below the clock tower since I was a boy, and I know exactly what that thin ground will and won't give. Greens and roots it gives; grain it grudges, and the Council's clerk counts only grain. So I sell my greens to Ruth Pike's kitchen and I pay what I can, and I will not beg any man for the difference. Let a quarryman's son come courting my Rosalind if he likes — she can wait a year and see sense.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: the terrace strips gave next to nothing and we ate the seed store down to the last sack.
The Council's clerk came round with the tithe book and would not write down a single bunch of greens, only grain.
Rosalind told me she means to marry Corwin Vance, and I told her to wait a year and see if he's still standing.
The cairn cutting on the ridge: the quarrymen broke into the giants' stones and now the shelf has shut its gate on us.
Verity and I planted the poor strip together the spring we married, and it came up better than anyone said it would.

Verity Ashcombe.narrative: I keep the terrace hens and the seed store, and I can tell you which strip will fail by the look of the soil in spring. Hedley frets at the tithe and the clerk's hard ledger, and I let him fret; I would trade eggs and roots against it tomorrow if the clerk would write them down. Rosalind is set on her new crop and her quarryman, and I say let the girl try — the poor ground will teach her what I cannot. Ottilie talks of nothing but the harbour, and I have not the heart to tell her I have never seen it either.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I rationed the seed store by the handful and the hens kept us alive when the strips gave nothing.
Rosalind came to me about Corwin Vance, and I told her a farmer's daughter can marry a quarryman if he's steady.
The Council's clerk counted only grain and would not write down a single basket of roots or eggs.
I taught Ottilie the names of the hens and which eggs to leave for setting.
The spring the poor strip came up green, Hedley laughed for the first time in months.

Rosalind Ashcombe.narrative: I work the terrace strips with my father, and I have a mind to try a new crop on the poor ground — clover and roots to hold the soil, whatever the old men say. I am courting Corwin Vance, and both our fathers have opinions they were not asked for; mine says wait a year, and Corwin's says a farmer's daughter is beneath a foreman's son. I am tired of the grumbling on both sides. The ground is the only thing here that tells the truth.

memories.gist: I told Father I meant to marry Corwin Vance, and he told me to wait a year as if I were a child.
Corwin walked me along the clock tower steps and said his father would come round; I am not so sure.
The Lean Year, when the strips failed and Mother rationed the seed store by the handful.
I sowed a patch of clover on the poor strip without telling Father, and it came up thick as a mat.
Silas Vance looked me up and down at the square and said nothing, which was worse than saying it.

stances.why: the poor ground needs clover and roots, not another year of the same failing grain

Ottilie Ashcombe.narrative: I drive the hens off the seed rows and help Mother with the eggs, and when the work is done I climb the clock tower steps and look south as far as I can see. They say Lanternquay is all neon and boats and tide lanterns lit for the drowned, and I have never been past the square. Rosalind says she will take me one day. I keep a gull's feather in my pocket for luck.
